why: A looks true to a candidate who reads the food and drink row instead of arcade games ((173 + 121) ÷ 402 = 73%); B looks true if tickets (+16%) is read in place of advertising beside food and drink (+17%); D is the over-reading from comparing margins (31% against 17%) or the 2012 profit alone instead of the whole period's; and the percentage-point slip (4 points against 2) makes C read false, so the correct option still tests it.

A holds against film and media alone (2%) rather than the rest of the market; C stretches farming's faster forecast growth without checking the starting levels; D comes from dividing 72 by the wrong column's total (72 ÷ 762 = 9.4%); and comparing total growth (7% against 65%) makes B read false.

B takes the second pie's 30% as a share of all respondents (wrong base), D reads 'main reason' as 'only reason', and C, about spending, is the one statement without basis that sourceHas lists; the wrong-base slip on A gives 60%, not 45%, so A still tests it.

B extends the fastest-growing segment's trend into the largest; C's 'twice' comes from comparing yearly absolute increases (0.66 against 0.3 a year, 2.2 times) instead of rates; D's 22% divides hybrid by the in-5-years column (7.5 ÷ 34); and absolute increases (2.3 against 1.3) make the correct option A read false.

$10.1bn reads bar 2's cumulative height (42% × $24bn), $19.6bn applies the step to the wrong base ($135bn × 14.5%), and $0.4bn applies it to Frostline's own $2.6bn sales (and is in any case covered by the numeric fillers that sourceHas lists); no slip lands on $3.5bn.

B (Hotel C's 5% conferences), C (Hotel C's 40% business) and D (Hotel C's 95%) each read one hotel's bar alone instead of the two hotels combined; the simple average (55%) and either single bar (50% or 60%) miss A's 57%, so A still tests both slips.
5.1% leaves out score 3 (23% × 22%), 2.4% does that on Question 2 (11% × 22%, two slips), and 1.2% is the answer off by a factor of 10 (a decimal slip in 0.54 × 0.22); no slip lands on 11.9%.

B, D, C, A and D, B, A, C each come from reading two brands' profits from each other's rows (or reversing one pairwise comparison), B, C, D, A is the single ranking filler that sourceHas lists, and ranking by profit alone landing on the correct option is the slip sourceHas names.

$1,750 prices the 1-litre bottle only, $350 also forgets the 5 bottles per crate, and $800 forgets the crate size on both sizes (average $775); the slips that still land on $4,000 (applying the 5% discount below the cut-off, $3,681; using one price per litre for both sizes, $4,375 or $3,750) are the ones sourceHas names.

2, 4, 3, 5, 1 ranks by absolute drop, 2, 1, 3, 4, 5 ranks by the 2014 level instead of the change, and 2, 4, 1, 5, 3 comes from misreading one of quintile 3's bars (for example taking its 2013 value 43 for 2014), which leaves it with no drop; dividing by the 2014 value landing on the correct ranking is the slip sourceHas names.
